node_notes.us_congress: Congress passed resolutions of support (1922 Lodge-Fish, the 1945 concurrent resolution) but never voted to create or recognize a state; those were executive acts. Named champions: Lodge, Fish, Wagner, Taft, Wright, Compton, Celler, Bloom; two-thirds of the Senate joined the American Palestine Committee. No documented campaign money from Zionist organizations to members of Congress before 1948 was found in the sources checked; the documented levers were letters, telegrams, platform planks and votes. The one documented campaign money in this map is Feinberg and Kaufmann's $100,000 for Truman in 1948.

edges.label: American Zionist leaders asked Lodge and Fish to introduce the resolution; the JVL credits the lobbying work of Rabbi Simon Glazer.
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge (R-Mass.) introduced the resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration.
Representative Hamilton Fish III (R-N.Y.) introduced it in the House.
The State Department (and the New York Times) opposed the resolution.
House passed it 30 June 1922; the Senate by unanimous consent 13 July 1922.
21 Sep 1922: Harding signed Public Resolution 67-73, favouring a national home and protecting the rights of "Christian and all other non-Jewish communities".
13 Jan 1922: Sokolow met Harding for nearly an hour during the Keren Hayesod tour (whether it touched the resolution is not recorded).
The resolution repeated the Balfour Declaration's phrase "a national home for the Jewish people".
Jan 1944: Rep. James Wright (D-Pa.) co-sponsored the House resolution for a "free and democratic Jewish commonwealth".
Rep. Ranulf Compton (R-Conn.) co-sponsored it.
Sen. Robert Wagner (D-N.Y.) sponsored the Senate version.
Sen. Robert Taft (R-Ohio) co-sponsored the Senate version.
Jan 1944: the Emergency Council's local committees began their first nationwide letter campaign for the resolutions.
Rabbi Morris Lazaron testified against: Zionism was an internal Jewish matter, not one for Congress.
Mar 1944: Army Chief of Staff Marshall asked Congress to postpone action for military reasons.
Mar 1944: Secretary of War Stimson opposed it on military grounds; it was put aside.
Oct 1944: Stimson wrote to Taft that political considerations now outweighed military ones; the objection was withdrawn days before the election.
Dec 1944: after House committee approval (30 Nov), action deferred again at the State Department's insistence.
Summer 1944: both parties adopted Palestine planks, "the first time in American history", by the council's own appraisal.
Taft chaired the Republican Resolutions Committee and invited Silver to give the convention benediction; the GOP plank called for "unrestricted immigration and land ownership".
Silver had a close relationship with Taft and lobbied Republican leaders on the plank.
Celler sat on the Democratic Resolutions Committee and backed Wise's push for a stronger plank; he warned the White House of Jewish voters' anger over the White Paper.
Wise lobbied Democratic delegates in Chicago for a plank to match the Republicans'.
Wise secured a meeting with Roosevelt, who weakened the Palestine statement Wise had drafted.
17 and 19 Dec 1945: both houses adopted a concurrent resolution, now calling for a "democratic commonwealth" with equal rights "regardless of race or creed".
The 1945 resolution had the American Palestine Committee's support.
And the Christian Council on Palestine's.
Rep. Emanuel Celler of Brooklyn, a leading House supporter.
Sol Bloom chaired the House Foreign Affairs Committee and was a leading supporter.
Bloom was a target of the council's telegram campaigns: it pressed allies as well as opponents.
June 1944: the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation registered as a foreign agent, naming the "Hebrew nation" as principal.
Hillel Kook ("Peter Bergson") led it and opened a "Hebrew Embassy" in Washington.
FBI files (FOIA, Wyman Institute): the Bergson investigation began at the State Department's instigation; informants, mail opening, trash searches.
An FBI memo: Bergson had "been in the hair of" Secretary of State Cordell Hull.
